headline: A boat maker turned down 400 million dollars

sources.title: He worked 100-hour weeks to save a nearly bankrupt boat company. At 83, he's just turned down $400 million for it
Grady-White's Owner Is Giving Away His Legendary Boat Company
Grady-White's Owner Turned Down $400 Million to Give the Company Away Instead
Instead of selling his luxury boat company for millions, he invested in his employees (video, CBS Evening News)

chunks.text: An 83-year-old American has {{turned down}} more than 400 million dollars for the company he built. Eddie Smith Jr. owns Grady-White Boats in Greenville, North Carolina, and buyers have spent years trying to get him to sell. In July 2026 he refused [[for the last time]]. [[Rather than]] {{hold on to}} the money himself, he has [[arranged]] things so that the company's [[profits]] will {{end up}} with [[charities]] instead.

verbs.why: You turn down an offer when you say no to it, even a very generous one. Smith turned down 400 million dollars because he wanted the company to stay independent.

verbs.wrong: To sell part of a company
verbs.why: Hold on to means to keep something for yourself instead of selling it. Smith could have held on to the profits, but he sent them to charity instead.

verbs.correct: To be somewhere in the end
verbs.why: End up describes where something finally lands, often without a clear plan getting it there. Here, the company's profits end up with charities instead of staying in Smith's own pocket.

chunks.text: Smith bought Grady-White in 1968, when he was 26 and the business was [[close to]] {{going under}}. He {{put in}} 80 to 100 hour weeks in those early years and stopped playing golf for [[decades]]. Over 58 years he {{built up}} a company that now earns hundreds of millions of dollars a year. He never sold shares to the public, never accepted [[outside investors]] and never {{took on}} any [[debt]]. During the [[boom]] of the 1970s he refused to grow the company by 300 or 400 percent, because he believed the boats would get worse.

verbs.wrong: To move to a bigger factory
verbs.why: A business goes under when its money is gone and it has to close. Grady-White was close to going under when Smith bought it in 1968.

verbs.wrong: To borrow money from a bank
verbs.why: When you put in long hours, you give a lot of time and effort to a job. Smith put in 80 to 100 hour weeks in the company's early years.

verbs.wrong: To design a new kind of boat
verbs.why: Build up means to grow something gradually, piece by piece, over a long time. Smith built up Grady-White over 58 years into a company worth hundreds of millions.
Take on means to accept a responsibility or burden, like a loan you now owe. Smith never took on debt, choosing instead to grow the company slowly with its own earnings.

chunks.text: What he has {{set up}} is unusual. The [[voting shares]] now sit in a [[trust]] that makes selling the company [[impossible]], so Grady-White should {{live on}} as an [[independent]] business. The other shares went to a charity that will {{give away}} tens of millions of dollars every year to education, [[healthcare]], [[conservation]] and [[local causes]]. Smith copied the idea from Yvon Chouinard, who handed the [[clothing company]] Patagonia to a similar trust in 2022.

verbs.wrong: To close a business for good
verbs.why: Set up means to create or arrange something so it is ready to work. Smith set up a trust structure that makes it impossible for anyone to sell the company.
Live on means to keep existing after the person who started it is gone. Thanks to the trust, Grady-White should live on as an independent company for many years.

verbs.wrong: To rent something for a year
verbs.why: Give away means to provide something for free, without asking anything in return. The charity will give away tens of millions of dollars a year to good causes.

chunks.text: About 350 people work at the single factory in Greenville. The company shares its profits with them, spends 350,000 to 400,000 dollars a year so that staff can read books, and employs a [[chaplain]]. Smith has {{stepped down}} to an [[honorary role]]. He did not {{pass down}} the company to his family, and he has had [[hard years]]: his wife Jo died in 2021 and his son Chris died of a [[nerve disease]] in 2022. He says a trust will {{look after}} the business better than any owner could. [[In his words]], by not selling, Grady-White will always be Grady-White.

verbs.why: Step down means to leave a position of power or responsibility, usually by your own choice. Smith stepped down to an honorary role after 58 years running the company.
Pass down means to give something, like a business or a tradition, to your children or grandchildren. Smith chose not to pass down Grady-White to his own family.

verbs.correct: To keep someone safe and well
verbs.wrong: To watch a person from far away
verbs.why: Look after means to protect and support someone or something over time. Smith believes a trust will look after the business better than any single owner could.

mainIdea.s: An 83-year-old boatbuilder in North Carolina turned down more than 400 million dollars for his company. He placed control in a trust and gave other shares to a charity that funds good causes.
mainIdea.why: He put the voting shares in a trust so the company cannot be sold, and gave the rest to a charity that funds causes.

mainIdea.s: The boatbuilder passed his company down to his son to keep it in the family permanently. He now holds an honorary role at the company he spent fifty eight years turning into a success.
mainIdea.why: Close, but he did not pass the company down to his family, and his son died in 2022.

mainIdea.s: A yacht manufacturer in Florida announced layoffs this year after a sharp drop in boat sales. The company blamed higher interest rates and rising costs for the sudden slowdown in demand.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a North Carolina boat company being given to a trust, not about layoffs in Florida.
